info.bio:
Charlie Christian (Charles Henry Christian) (29 de julio de 1926 - 2 de marzo de 1942) guitarrista de jazz (swing y bebop) estadounidense.

      Charlie Christian, nació en el seno de una familia respetable de Dallas y en ambiente musical muy profundo. Su padre era guitarrista y cantante de blues y ello junto a sus estudios en la "Douglas School"  contribuyó poderosamente a crear en el una amplia base musical. Sus influencia primarias fueron músicos de jazz de visita a su ciudad natal

scenes.name: Charlie Christian y la guitarra eléctrica
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Un chico de Oklahoma City que tocaba en el Ritz Cafe por siete dólares y medio, recomendado por Mary Lou Williams a John Hammond: Goodman lo desdeña («un palurdo increíble») hasta que improvisan una hora sobre «Rose Room». En menos de dos años de grabaciones con el sexteto de Goodman define la guitarra eléctrica en el jazz con líneas de una sola nota, saltos interválicos, tresillos y tensiones cromáticas, frases que los guitarristas copiarán como un canon. Sus noches en el Minton's lo convierten en pionero del bebop; la tuberculosis lo mata en 1942.

Para aquella generación la electricidad era un simple elemento práctico, relacionado con las farolas y los pararrayos, pero no con la interpretación musical. podcast.title: Meeting Les Paul (1938)
podcast.body: Charlie Christian met Les Paul at a Bob Wills gig in Tulsa, Oklahoma, in 1938. Paul, impressed by Christian's guitar playing, invited him to jam with the band on stage, marking their first encounter shortly before Christian joined Benny Goodman's band. "That was the first time that Les Paul met his friend Charlie Christian, shortly before Christian got the offer from Benny Goodman, hanging out and jamming at a Bob Willes gig."

podcast.title: Early Death (1941)
podcast.body: Charlie Christian suffered from tuberculosis as early as 1939 when "Flying Home" was recorded, and he tragically died on March 2, 1941, at the young age of 25. His grave remained unmarked for 53 years, and even a later memorial was placed incorrectly, underscoring his underappreciated legacy. "And on March 2, 1941, aged only 25, Charlie Christian died."

podcast.title: Coined "B-bop" Name
podcast.body: Christian was responsible for the name "B-bop" being given to the form of music he helped create in jam sessions after his regular work. This demonstrates his deep involvement in the early development of a new jazz subgenre. "While Christian was responsible for their name B-bop, being given to the form of music, he helped create in jam sessions after his regular work."

podcast.title: Discovery by John Hammond
podcast.body: John Hammond, a talent scout for Benny Goodman's Big Band Orchestra, convinced Benny Goodman to give Charlie Christian an audition, despite Goodman's initial skepticism about the electric guitar. Goodman was ultimately impressed by Christian's skill on the Gibson ES150. "John Hammond, a talent scout for Benny Goodman's Big Band Orchestra, armed twisted Benny into giving Charlie a shot. Goodman wasn't really into it because, well, who the hell wants to hear an electric guitar, he apparently said. But because Goodman trusted Hammond, he agreed to at least listen to Charlie. He was blown away by his abilities on this new instrument, which was a Gibson ES150 Spanish-style electric guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Early Electric Guitar Soloing
podcast.body: Charlie Christian was an excellent guitarist who saw the potential for the electric guitar beyond chords and rhythm. He started improvising solos in jam sessions as early as 1931 and, after joining Benny Goodman's big band in 1939, was given the freedom to solo extensively, transforming the amplified guitar's role. "In 1931, he started soloing during jam sessions with fellow musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Rockabilly Style
podcast.body: Christian's soloing on "Flying Home," characterized by short bursts of single-note guitar lines, is effectively rockabilly and is compared to the playing of Scotty Moore 16 years later. This was revolutionary at a time when the guitar was predominantly a rhythm instrument in jazz. "Christian's short bursts of single note guitar line are, to all intents and purposes, rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Electric Guitar Pioneer
podcast.body: Charlie Christian was a pioneer of the electric guitar, significantly elevating its prominence as a solo instrument. While he was not the first electric guitarist, nor the first to record it, his innovative playing fundamentally changed the approach to guitar in popular music by allowing it to play loud, single melody lines on par with horns. "Christian is sometimes erroneously called the first electric guitarist, or the first person to play electric guitar on record, or even the inventor of the electric guitar. He was none of those things, but he was a pioneer in the instrument, and the first person to really bring it to prominence as a solo instrument."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: First Guitar Hero
podcast.body: Charlie Christian, a Black man from Oklahoma, is recognized as the world's first guitar hero for his pioneering use of the electric guitar. He began soloing during jam sessions in 1931, acquired an electric guitar in 1936, and by 1939 with Benny Goodman's big band, was allowed to improvise and solo during performances, laying the foundations for the lead guitarist role. "So by every measure you want to use, Charlie Christian was the world's first guitar hero."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Guitar Hero
podcast.body: After joining Benny Goodman's orchestra with his Gibson ES150, Charlie Christian rapidly achieved stardom, earning the title of the first-ever guitar hero. His performances left audiences in disbelief, and his influence significantly increased the demand for electric guitars, leading to more manufacturers entering the market by the early 1940s. "Once Charlie joined Goodman's orchestra with his Gibson, he became a star, the first ever guitar hero. Anyone who saw or heard Charlie with Benny Goodman's orchestra couldn't believe what they were hearing. After Charlie Christian, demand for the electric guitars went way up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Bop
podcast.body: Christian was a huge influence on Bop music, which would emerge many years after his death. His advanced technique and unique amplified sound were foundational to the genre's development. "He was a huge influence on Bop, which wouldn't come along for many more years, and in just the sound of it."

podcast.title: Influence on Chuck Berry
podcast.body: Chuck Berry later identified Christian as one of the biggest influences on his guitar playing, though Berry mistakenly believed Christian played with Tommy Dorsey's band rather than Goodman's. This highlights Christian's profound, albeit sometimes misattributed, impact on early rock and roll guitarists. "Chuck Berry later said the Christian was one of the biggest influences on his guitar playing, though he wrongly said the Christian played with Tommy Dorses band, arrival to Goodman's."

podcast.title: Tragic Early Death
podcast.body: Charlie Christian's profound influence on music was cut short when he died of tuberculosis on March 3, 1941, at the young age of 25. He did not live to see the full extent of the electric guitar's future development and impact. "Sadly, Charlie didn't get to see what became of the electric guitar. He died of tuberculosis on March 3rd, 1941, at the age of 25. Still, the first guitar hero, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Untimely Death and Legacy
podcast.body: Christian died young from tuberculosis on March 3rd, 1941, at the age of 25. Despite his short career, he is credited with taking the amplified guitar out of the shadows and establishing the foundational role of the lead guitarist in modern music. "Until he died of tuberculosis on March 3rd, 1941 at the age of 25, Charlie took the new amplified guitar out of the shadows and is now recognized as the person to create the foundations of the lead guitarist as we know it today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence of Charlie Christian on Electric Guitar Design
xref.body: In 1939, likely inspired by hearing Charlie Christian play, Les Paul conceived his own design for an electric guitar, which he dubbed "the log." This marked a significant shift in his focus towards electrification. "But in 1939, most likely after hearing Charlie Christian, he came up with an idea for his own electric guitar design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Skepticism about Electric Guitar
xref.body: Benny Goodman initially expressed strong reservations about the electric guitar, questioning its musical relevance before being persuaded by talent scout John Hammond to audition Charlie Christian. His reaction highlights the novelty and unfamiliarity of the instrument at the time. "Goodman wasn't really into it because, well, who the hell wants to hear an electric guitar, he apparently said."
